meta.title: Who really said "I owe the public nothing"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: J. P. Morgan really said it — to a correspondent in Paris in May 1901, refusing to comment on the Northern Pacific panic. The printed exchange survives.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I owe the public nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes — Morgan said it. Asked if he owed the public a statement on the 1901 panic, he answered in five words. The full exchange is in a May 1901 newspaper.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Morgan really said it — in Paris, in May 1901, brushing off a correspondent who asked whether he owed the public a statement about the Northern Pacific panic. The full exchange is printed verbatim in The Guthrie Daily Leader of 15 May 1901, and the scanned page is legible today.

source.heading: The exchange, as printed

docMeta.dd: 15 May 1901, page 2 — Paris dispatch headed “Morgan in a Rage”
Refusing comment on the Northern Pacific corner panic
New York World, 11 May 1901 (Wikiquote, after Jean Strouse)

source.excerpt:
“But, Mr. Morgan,” the correspondent protested, “you told me yesterday to come again.” Morgan’s response was a grunt.
“Don’t you think,” the correspondent asked, “that since you are being blamed for a panic that has ruined thousands of people and disturbed a whole nation, some statement is due to the public?”
“I owe the public nothing,” Morgan retorted.
“Won’t you say whether you consider yourself responsible?”
“I will say nothing.”
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section for Morgan carries the line with a citation rather than a shrug: “Quoted in the New York World (11 May 1901) during the Northern Pacific Corner,” referred to Jean Strouse’s Morgan: American Financier. Wikiquote ↗

The exchange itself survives in print. A Paris cable headed “Morgan in a Rage” ran in The Guthrie Daily Leader of 15 May 1901, page 2, and the scan shows the words plainly: “I owe the public nothing,” Morgan retorted. Library of Congress ↗
The occasion checks out: Harriman and Schiff against Morgan and Hill for control of the Northern Pacific Railway, with the market crashing on the afternoon of 8 May 1901. Panic of 1901 ↗
So does the temperament. Morgan disliked publicity and hated being photographed without his permission, which is the same man who answers a reporter with a grunt and then five words. Wikipedia ↗
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned page at the Library of Congress; the words above are legible in the newspaper image itself, not only in the machine-read text. Wikiquote cites the same line to the New York World of 11 May 1901 — four days before this printing — and we have not been able to inspect that issue.

author.name: J. P. Morgan
author.heading: About J. P. Morgan
author.bio: John Pierpont Morgan was the American financier and investment banker who dominated corporate finance on Wall Street through the Gilded Age and the Progressive Era. He disliked publicity and hated being photographed without his permission — a temperament that makes a five-word brush-off to a reporter entirely in character. The railroad truce he brokered after the 1901 fight became the Northern Securities Company, which the Supreme Court dissolved in 1904.

cite.sourceCitation: “Morgan in a Rage: Said to Have Blamed His New York Partners For the Panic,” The Guthrie Daily Leader (Guthrie, Okla.), 15 May 1901, p. 2 (Paris dispatch), Chronicling America, Library of Congress. Wikiquote cites the same line to the New York World, 11 May 1901, following Jean Strouse’s Morgan: American Financier.

misattribution.heading: How the line goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound — this one really is Morgan’s. What goes wrong is everything around it: the question it answered, the paper it ran in, and the other Gilded Age snub it keeps getting swapped for.

items.scope: The line it gets swapped with
items.why: “The public be damned!” is Vanderbilt’s, from an 1882 railroad interview — and it is the less secure of the two. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Disputed, records that Vanderbilt promptly denied it, and notes that the earliest version appears in the Chicago Herald of 9 October 1882 with the accounts varying widely. Morgan’s five words are the ones with a printed exchange behind them.

items.who: J. P. Morgan — correctly named, but for a creed he never stated
items.why: Quote walls print it bare: picturequotes.com ↗ gives the line and the name and nothing else, which lets it read as a philosophy of wealth. In the source it is narrower and colder than that — a refusal to give a press statement, followed immediately by “I will say nothing.”

Wikiquote ↗, following Jean Strouse’s Morgan: American Financier, dates the printing to the New York World of 11 May 1901. The syndicated text we could actually read is datelined Paris and ran on 15 May 1901. We have not inspected the World itself, so we cite the printing we could read and flag the difference rather than smooth it over.

misattribution.truthLine: What Morgan actually said, in Paris in May 1901, was a refusal. Asked whether he owed a statement to the public over a panic that had “ruined thousands of people and disturbed a whole nation,” he answered “I owe the public nothing” — and then “I will say nothing.” The Guthrie Daily Leader, 15 May 1901 ↗

context.heading: Why he was being asked
lead: In the first days of May 1901 two camps — E. H. Harriman with Jacob Schiff on one side, J. P. Morgan with James J. Hill on the other — were quietly buying the same railway. They bought so much Northern Pacific between them that the traders who had sold it short could not find shares to deliver, and on the afternoon of 8 May the stock market crashed ↗. Morgan was not there for any of it. He was taking the cure at Aix-les-Bains, and, as the dispatch put it, his partners had taken advantage of his being “almost beyond reach.”

By the time he reached his Paris bank he was, per the headline, in a rage — the correspondent reports him denouncing his New York partners “alternately as a lot of idiots and a pack of rascals.” The next afternoon a reporter caught him walking into his hotel and put the obvious question. That is the moment the five famous words belong to: not a philosophy of wealth, but a man declining to give a press statement about a panic he was being blamed for.
detailsBody: Morgan cut his European trip short. The same dispatch has him telling the correspondent he was leaving the next morning for London and sailing home from Liverpool on the Teutonic.

The railway fight was settled by merging the combatants’ interests into the Northern Securities Company. That truce drew the attention of President Theodore Roosevelt, and in 1904 the Supreme Court dissolved the company ↗. Morgan did not lose money on it; his political reputation did not fare as well.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced Quotes section for J. P. Morgan lists "I owe the public nothing." with the citation "Quoted in the New York World (11 May 1901) during the Northern Pacific Corner. See Morgan: American Financier by Jean Strouse". The page's other sections are Testimony to the Pujo Committee (1912), Attributed, Quotes about Morgan and External links.

The Guthrie Daily Leader (Guthrie, Okla.), 15 May 1901, page 2, prints a Paris-datelined dispatch headed "MORGAN IN A RAGE / Said to Have Blamed His New York Partners For the Panic" containing verbatim: the correspondent asking whether "since you are being blamed for a panic that has ruined thousands of people and disturbed a whole nation, some statement is due to the public?"; "I owe the public nothing," Morgan retorted; "Won't you say whether you consider yourself responsible?"; "I will say nothing." It also states his partners acted while he was "away at Aix-les-Bains and almost beyond reach", that he denounced them "as a lot of idiots and a pack of rascals", that he arrived at Morgan, Harjes & Co. on the boulevard Haussmann, and that he was leaving for London and sailing on the Teutonic from Liverpool. Verified via the LOC resource JSON, the ALTO full text, and by reading the IIIF page scan directly.

Wikiquote files William Henry Vanderbilt's "The public be damned!" under its Disputed section, notes it was an attributed remark to a reporter promptly denied by Vanderbilt, that descriptions of the context vary widely, and that the earliest version appears in the Chicago Herald of 9 October 1882.

J. P. Morgan was born 17 April 1837 and died 31 March 1913; he was an American financier and investment banker who dominated corporate finance on Wall Street throughout the Gilded Age and Progressive Era; he disliked publicity and hated being photographed without his permission; in 1904 the Supreme Court dissolved the Northern Securities Company, and though he did not lose money his political reputation suffered.

The Panic of 1901 was caused in part by struggles between E. H. Harriman, Jacob Schiff, and J. P. Morgan/James J. Hill for financial control of the Northern Pacific Railway, and the stock market crashed during the afternoon of 8 May 1901.

American Heritage's article recounts the May 1901 Northern Pacific corner and the resulting market chaos; it contains no direct quotation from J. P. Morgan and does not include the phrase "I owe the public nothing".
picturequotes.com displays "I owe the public nothing" with only the author's name and no source, date, publication or context.
